newsitem.title: HAITI: Violence, arson continue in Haiti slum.
newsitem.headline: Violence, arson continue in Haiti slum.

text.p: At least one person was wounded and some 56 houses were burned in gang warfare in a Port-au-Prince slum on Thursday, police said.
Meanwhile, two top U.S. security officials were due to arrive in the city on Thursday to discuss ways to make the impoverished Caribbean nation more attractive to investors.

Rival gangs from different sections of Cite Soleil, the slum home of 200,000 of Haiti's poorest residents, have terrorised the area in the past week, leaving at least 11 dead, dozens wounded and an estimated 100 houses burned.

"These men came into my house and they started shooting and breaking everything. Then they set my house on fire and I have nowhere else to go," said Miralda Dissan, who was crying and throwing water on her shack, which was still smouldering.
U.N. troops, civilian police trainers, U.S. Marines and the Haitian National Police and their SWAT-style rapid response team were trying to secure the area on Thursday morning.
"From day to day, we never know what is going to happen here," said civilian police trainer Tony Farahbakh. "It is so dangerous and unpredictable."
Frightened residents who had somewhere else to go were packing their bags to leave the slum, saying they had not slept since the gunfire began last weekend.

Police and eyewitnesses said gang members were roaming through streets and back alleys armed with pistols and automatic weapons. Police were questioning how the gang members aqcuired such an arsenal in an area where most people barely have enough money for adequate food and other necessities.

Such high-profile violence and the pending end of the U.N. peacekeeping mission in July do little to make Haiti appeal to international investors, which government officials say is badly needed to stimulate the impoverished nation's economy.
U.S. National Security Advisor Samuel Berger and Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott were scheduled to arrive in Haiti sometime on Thursday.
According to the White House, Berger and Talbott's visit was to include discussions with President Rene Preval about "the need to rapidly create conditions attractive to investors."
Other matters to be discussed in the meeting with Preval include the need to resolve several recent political assassinations and strengthen Haiti's weak justice system, a White House official said.
